blocks.purpose: Left/right swipes judging statements about end-focus, fronting, and emphasis, retrieving the word-order rules by recognition.

data.instruction: Swipe right if the statement is true, left if it is false.

statements.feedback: End-focus: the last position is where the reader's attention lands.
statements.text: What a reader meets first and last carries the most weight.

statements.feedback: Fronting spotlights whatever you move to the start.
statements.text: Fronting means moving a word or phrase to the start of the sentence to spotlight it.

statements.feedback: Fronting puts the moved phrase FIRST; the point saved for last is the periodic pattern.
statements.text: Fronting saves the important idea for the very end of the sentence.

statements.feedback: End-focus: 'without a trace' gets the final emphasis.
statements.text: 'She left without a trace' puts its emphasis on 'without a trace'.

statements.feedback: Parallel structure earns credibility; only matching forms create the rhythm.
statements.text: Parallel structure works best when the matching phrases use different grammatical forms.

statements.feedback: Readers naturally give extra weight to what they read first — so front it deliberately.
statements.text: Moving a key phrase to the front makes the reader meet it before anything else.

statements.feedback: Deliberate fragments get their punch from breaking the rule on purpose, not from hiding errors.
statements.text: A deliberate fragment is just an accidental fragment that went unnoticed.

statements.feedback: The first and last slots are the strongest positions in a sentence.
statements.text: When you rewrite for emphasis, put your strongest words in the first or last position.

data.summaryBody: First and last positions carry the most weight. Fronting spotlights a phrase by moving it to the start; parallel structure builds rhythm through matching forms. And a fragment is only deliberate when the break is the point.
data.title: Recall: Word Order and Emphasis

blocks.purpose: A tempting choice set where the 'wrong' answer is a run-on rewritten as a fragment or vice versa, so the learner must apply the boundary, not pattern-match.

options.text: Delete the period: 'Fear is a reasonable response to danger panic is not.' — keep it as one flowing sentence.
options.whyNot: This makes the run-on worse. Fusing two complete sentences with no punctuation at all is exactly the error that blurs the argument; the reader crashes into 'panic' with no signal.

options.text: Split it: 'Fear is a reasonable response to danger. Panic is not.' Then add a deliberate fragment if you want extra punch: 'Not panic.'
options.whyNot: Survives scrutiny: it fixes the run-on with a period, restores clear end-focus on 'not', and the optional deliberate fragment adds punch on purpose — the boundary between accident and choice is respected.

options.text: Replace the period with a comma: 'Fear is a reasonable response to danger, panic is not.'
options.whyNot: That's a comma splice — a comma alone can't join two complete sentences, so this is still a run-on, just with a comma painted on top.

options.text: Turn the second half into a fragment: 'Fear is a reasonable response to danger. Panic is not.' but delete 'Panic' so it reads '...to danger. Is not.'
options.whyNot: It deletes the subject 'Panic', leaving 'Is not.' with nothing to refer to — an accidental fragment, not a deliberate one, because the reader can't recover the missing subject.

checks.prompt: Classify this item: 'The concert sold out instantly, fans camped outside for tickets, nobody complained about the price.'
checks.rationale: Every clause is complete, and they're joined only by commas — three comma splices make this a run-on, not a fragment or a deliberate stylistic break.
checks.hint: Ask: could each half stand alone as a sentence? If yes and they're fused, you know the answer.
checks.focus: Classify a tricky sentence as fragment, run-on, or deliberate fragment

checks.prompt: The flat sentence 'She closed the door quietly.' is rewritten four ways. Which rewrite uses fronting to put the emphasis on 'quietly'?
checks.rationale: Fronting moves 'Quietly' to the very start, so the reader meets it first — that's the position fronting uses to spotlight a word.
checks.hint: Fronting puts the spotlighted word in the first position.
choices: She quietly closed the door, and she did it fast.
The door was closed by her, quietly.
checks.focus: End-focus: which rewritten sentence puts emphasis on the right word

checks.prompt: 'Fear is a reasonable response to danger panic is not.' Why does the run-on weaken the argument, and which fix is correct?
checks.answer: Period after 'danger', then the deliberate fragment 'Not panic.'
checks.rationale: A run-on blurs where one claim ends and the next begins, dropping the impact; a period restores end-focus on 'not', and the optional deliberate fragment adds punch without deleting the subject.
checks.hint: A comma can't join two full sentences, and a deliberate fragment still needs to be recoverable.
choices: Comma splice: put a comma after 'danger'
Delete the period and run both clauses together
Period after 'danger', then the deliberate fragment 'Not panic.'
checks.focus: Why a run-on weakens persuasion and which fix is correct

checks.prompt: 'Although the storm knocked out the power and flooded the roads, the town never stopped working.' Is this order periodic or cumulative? Answer with one word.
checks.rationale: The dependent clauses delay the main point ('the town never stopped working') until the end — that build-up to a point is the definition of periodic order.
checks.hint: Where does the main point land — the beginning or the end?
checks.focus: Distinguish periodic vs cumulative order in a sentence

checks.prompt: Here is the paragraph's run-on: 'The volunteers cleared the beach the research team recorded the results and everyone agreed the project was a success, the opposite of what critics predicted.' What is the exact punctuation fix?
checks.rationale: The run-on fuses 'the project was a success' with 'the opposite of what critics predicted'; a period after 'success' splits them into two complete sentences.
checks.hint: The fix must separate two complete sentences with a full stop.
checks.focus: Identify the exact punctuation fix for the paragraph's run-on

checks.prompt: Rewrite this flat sentence using fronting: 'She signed the contract without hesitation.' Write the full fronted version.
checks.answer: Without hesitation, she signed the contract.
checks.rationale: Fronting means moving the key phrase to the start of the sentence so the reader meets it first.
accepts: Without hesitation, she signed the contract.
Without hesitation she signed the contract.
checks.hint: Move the spotlighted phrase to the very start, before the subject.
checks.focus: Rewrite a flat sentence with fronting or parallel structure for emphasis
